keep: The idea is named in one line up front: a pump gives the water lift plus friction, both as head, friction grows with flow squared, and head × flow sets the power and the motor's current.
Head is built from Pressure in liquids backwards, h = p ÷ ρg, worked in seawater (100 kPa is about 9.9 m), and given its energy meaning, 1 J per newton per metre.
Darcy's rule is stated in words and worked with real numbers: 50 m of 50 mm pipe at f = 0.02 loses about 4.1 m at 2 m/s and about 16.3 m at 4 m/s.
The power chain divides at each link with a causal reason and ends on the ammeter Dan reads: 2.01 kW, 2.87 kW, 3.19 kW, about 4.9 A on 440 V three-phase.

The picture is the brief's system curve builder: lift, length, bore and flow; a lift bar that never moves under a friction bar that grows as flow squared; dots tracing the system curve; the chain to an ammeter. Its opening settings land on the same 10 L/s and 20 m as the worked example.

Every misconception in the brief for this lesson has a DO screen with a wrong pick of its own: head without ρg (screen 2, 195 m), friction in step with flow (screens 4 and 8), multiplying by an efficiency (screens 10 and 12). The mixed puzzles reach back to continuity (screen 13) and lesson 5's relative density.

The analogy, charging a battery through long leads, reproduces the main result (fixed EMF plus a drop that grows with current, power = V × I) and its breaks names the real difference: a lead's drop is linear in current and goes with 1 ÷ D², pipe friction with flow squared and far more steeply with bore.
fix: Causal step presented as sourced fact: 'Over each stretch of pipe the eddies scrub off a share of it' is a picture of why, not in the research. Mark it 'One way to picture why:' and say the energy becomes heat.
False absolute: 'it is the same at any flow, even none' holds only while the tanks' levels hold. Say so.
The misconception is not shown failing in the explanation: add that many expect twice the speed to lose twice the head, and it loses four times.
The research quote [1] says head is the height a pump can raise fluid, not that makers rate pumps by it. Reword the footnoted sentence to what the quote supports.
The teaching model is not named: say once that this is a simplified model, that real pipes add bends and valves and a real f shifts a little with speed.
The efficiency step gives no reason why it divides: add that each stage takes in more than it passes on, and that the pump wastes some of what its shaft gives it.
One sentence chains two actions with 'and' ('It must lift it ..., and push it ...'): split into two short sentences; state that L and D are both in metres.
